CAPTION QUALITY CHECKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Do your captions read too fast, too crowded, or off-sync?

Paste an SRT or WebVTT caption file and check every cue's reading speed, line length, lines per cue, on-screen duration, and timing (overlaps, too-short gaps, invalid or out-of-order cues) against commonly-used caption style-guide thresholds.

Nothing is uploaded. The caption text you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device.

1. Check a caption file

Paste the whole file, including the WEBVTT header for a VTT track, or the numeric cue index for an SRT track.

2. Report

0cues 0danger 0notice

Findings

Per-cue metrics

#StartDurationCharsCPSLinesText

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

The CLI reads a local .srt/.vtt file and runs the identical checks — no browser, no upload, nothing goes through this site:

node check.mjs captions.srt --json
node check.mjs captions.vtt --max-cps 17
node check.mjs captions.srt --max-line-length 32 --max-lines 2

Get check.mjs and engine.mjs from the repo — plain Node 18+, nothing to install. Exit code 1 when a danger-severity finding is produced (reading too fast, overlapping cues, invalid or out-of-order timing) or the file cannot be read at all.

What's checked

CheckWhat it flagsSeverity
Reading too fastCharacters per second above the cap (default 20)Danger
Invalid timingA cue's end time is at or before its start timeDanger
Out of orderA cue starts before an earlier one in the fileDanger
Overlapping cuesA cue's end time is after the next cue's start timeDanger
Duration too shortOn screen for less than the minimum (default 5/6 second)Notice
Duration too longOn screen for more than the maximum (default 7 seconds)Notice
Line too longA line above the maximum length (default 42 characters)Notice
Too many linesMore lines in one cue than the maximum (default 2)Notice
Gap too shortLess than the minimum gap (default ~84ms) between two cuesNotice
Empty cueA cue with no visible text at allNotice

More: why caption quality is a separate question from caption presence, and where these thresholds come from.

Common questions

What counts as "too fast" for captions?

There is no single legal reading-speed limit, but caption style guides converge on a similar range: a commonly-cited ceiling for adult-content captions is around 20 characters per second (roughly 160-180 words per minute), with a lower cap often used for children's content. This tool defaults to 20 characters per second and lets you lower or raise it with --max-cps on the CLI.

Why does caption quality matter if WCAG only requires that captions exist?

WCAG Success Criterion 1.2.2 requires captions for prerecorded audio content, but it does not grade how readable those captions are once they exist. A caption track can be technically present — it parses, it plays, it is synced — and still fail the viewer it exists for if the text moves faster than a typical reading speed, crowds too many lines into the frame, or flickers past in under a second. Quality is a separate, unenforced question from presence, and this tool checks the quality question.

Where do the specific numbers (42 characters per line, two lines, 20 cps) come from?

They are commonly-used industry thresholds, not one single controlling standard — publicly published caption style guides such as Netflix's Timed Text Style Guide and the BBC's Subtitle Guidelines state versions of these same numbers (reading speed caps, a two-line maximum, minimum and maximum on-screen duration). This tool cites them as widely-used defaults and makes every threshold configurable on the CLI, because a specific broadcaster, platform, or client contract may set its own numbers.

Does this replace a human caption review?

No. It checks mechanically verifiable properties of the timing and text you provide — reading speed, line length, duration, overlap, and gaps. It cannot judge whether a caption is an accurate transcription, whether speaker labels or sound descriptions are used correctly, or whether the translation (for subtitles) reads naturally. Treat a clean report as evidence that the mechanical thresholds are met, not as a substitute for reviewing the captions yourself.

It is not legal, accessibility-compliance, or broadcast-standards advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or a human caption review. It reports whether the caption file you provided satisfies specific, mechanically checkable, commonly-used thresholds — nothing more, and not a certification of WCAG, FCC, or any other standard's compliance. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything you paste runs in your browser and is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a look if captioning is part of a broader accessibility push: ADA Title II Evidence and Shopify Accessibility Evidence both produce disclosed, evidence-based accessibility records rather than a compliance guarantee.

vs-professional-caption-qc-review.html.text:
← Caption Quality Checker

This checker vs. a paid captioning vendor's QC pass

A managed captioning vendor's QC pass is a human reviewer bundled into the price of a captioning job: they check whether the transcription is accurate, whether speaker labels and sound descriptions are used correctly, and whether a translated subtitle reads naturally. That review is valuable and this tool does not attempt to replace it — but it costs money per project, is not instant, and needs your media or caption file uploaded to that vendor's platform.

This tool checks a narrower, purely mechanical slice of caption quality — reading speed, line length, lines per cue, on-screen duration, overlapping cues, and timing — against commonly-used caption style-guide thresholds. It runs instantly, for free, from pasted text in your browser or a local file on the CLI, and nothing you check is ever uploaded anywhere.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is this caption file's transcription actually accurate? A human review, such as a captioning vendor's QC pass — this tool has no model of meaning and cannot judge accuracy.
Does every cue meet a stated reading-speed cap, line-length limit, and duration range? This checker — a deterministic, repeatable answer in seconds, free.
Are speaker labels, sound descriptions, or a translation's wording correct? A human reviewer — outside what mechanical checks can verify.
I want this run automatically on every caption file before a human ever reviews it. This checker's CLI — wireable into your own CI, exits non-zero on a danger-severity finding.
I'd rather not upload my caption file to a third party for a quick pacing check. This checker — runs entirely in your browser or on your own machine; nothing is uploaded.

Neither replaces the other. A vendor's QC pass is what catches whether the words are right. This tool is what catches whether the timing and formatting are right — cheaply, instantly, and as many times as you want, before or instead of paying for a human pass on the mechanical half of the job.

Common questions

Should I use this tool instead of paying for a professional captioning QC pass?

Different jobs, and they are often used together. A paid captioning vendor's QC pass is a human review bundled into the cost of a managed captioning job — checking whether the transcription is accurate, whether speaker labels and sound descriptions are used correctly, and whether a translation reads naturally. This tool checks a narrower, purely mechanical set of properties — reading speed, line length, on-screen duration, overlaps, and timing — instantly and for free, on a file you already have. It does not replace a human accuracy review; it catches the pacing and formatting problems a human reviewer would otherwise have to check by eye.

What can a paid vendor's QC pass catch that this tool can't?

Anything that requires understanding meaning rather than measuring timestamps and character counts: whether the transcription is actually correct, whether a speaker change is labelled, whether a sound description is accurate, or whether a translated subtitle reads naturally in the target language. This tool has no model of meaning at all — it only measures mechanically verifiable properties of the cues you give it.

What can this tool catch that a general QC pass might not guarantee?

A specific, numeric, repeatable answer to whether every cue meets a stated reading-speed cap, line-length limit, and duration range — the kind of check that is tedious and error-prone for a human to do cue-by-cue by eye, and that a vendor's QC process may or may not check against the same numbers you care about. Because it is deterministic arithmetic, running it twice on the same file always gives the same answer, and you can wire it into your own CI so it runs on every caption file before a human ever sees it.

Is my caption file uploaded anywhere when I use this tool?

No. The browser page parses whatever text you paste in your own browser and never sends it anywhere; the CLI reads a local file directly from your own disk. A managed captioning vendor's QC pass, by contrast, necessarily involves sending your media or caption file to that vendor's platform for a human to review — that upload is a normal and unavoidable part of how a human review works, and it is one difference this free, local tool is specifically built to avoid for the mechanical checks it does run.

why-caption-quality-matters.html.text:
← Caption Quality Checker

Why caption quality is a different question from caption presence

WCAG Success Criterion 1.2.2 requires captions for prerecorded audio content. Section 508 and a growing list of state and international accessibility rules point back to the same requirement. None of them grade the captions once they exist. A track can satisfy every "does it have captions" check in existence and still be unreadable to the person it was made for.

Presence is a checkbox. Readability is arithmetic.

A caption file passes "presence" the moment it parses, syncs to the video, and displays something. None of that says whether a viewer can actually read a given cue before it changes. That is a function of exactly two numbers — how many characters are on screen, and for how long — and a caption track can fail it while being a perfectly accurate transcription of the audio.

Why automatic captions make this worse, not better

Automatic speech recognition optimizes for transcription accuracy: getting the words right. It has no model of how fast a human reads. It breaks caption blocks on pauses in the audio track, not on a target character count, so a dense, fast-talking passage produces a caption block that is word-for-word correct and reads at a speed nobody can follow. The rise of auto-captioning has made "does it exist" trivially easy and "is it readable" no more solved than before — if anything, the gap between the two questions has gotten wider, not narrower.

Where the specific numbers come from

There is no single legal reading-speed limit the way there is a legal blood-alcohol limit. What exists instead is a convergent set of numbers across several independently-published caption style guides — Netflix's public Timed Text Style Guide and the BBC's Subtitle Guidelines both publish figures in the same neighborhood: a reading-speed ceiling in the high teens to low twenties of characters per second, a two-line maximum per cue, and minimum/maximum on-screen durations in roughly the same range. None of these guides has legal force outside its own platform's contracts. They are cited here as commonly-used industry defaults, not as one controlling standard — which is also why every threshold in this tool is configurable.

The trade-off a longer duration doesn't escape

Stretching a cue's on-screen time lowers its characters-per-second reading speed, and it is the first fix most people reach for. It has a ceiling: a cue left on screen too long (past a commonly-used ceiling around seven seconds) invites the viewer to re-read it, and by then the dialogue and the picture have both moved on — the caption stops matching what is happening on screen. When a line is genuinely too dense to read in a reasonable time, the more durable fix is usually to shorten the wording, not to hold the cue open longer.

Checking this mechanically rather than by eye

Reading speed, line length, lines per cue, minimum/maximum duration, overlaps, and gaps are all mechanically computable from the timestamps and text a caption file already contains — no judgment call, no audio needed. Caption Quality Checker runs those checks: paste an SRT or WebVTT file, or run the CLI against a file on disk and wire it into CI as a regression gate on every future upload.

Common questions

Isn't an auto-generated caption track already "good enough" if it's accurate?

Accuracy and readability are two different properties, and an automatic speech-recognition system optimizes for accuracy, not for the pacing a human reads at. It breaks cues on pauses in the audio, not on a target reading speed — so a fast talker can produce a caption block dense enough to be technically correct and still impossible to finish reading before the next cue replaces it. The transcription can be word-for-word right and the caption track can still fail its own audience.

Who actually checks caption quality today?

Usually nobody, mechanically. A video platform's own upload validator checks that a caption file parses and that timestamps are well-formed — it has no opinion on whether a cue is readable in the time given. A human style-guide reviewer at a large broadcaster or streaming platform checks this by eye, cue by cue, which is exactly the kind of repetitive check a deterministic tool should be doing before a human ever looks at the file.

Does a longer duration always fix a reading-speed problem?

Only up to a point, and it trades one problem for another. Stretching a cue's duration lowers its characters-per-second, but a cue left on screen for too long (past the commonly-used ~7-second ceiling) invites re-reading and desyncs the viewer's attention from the picture — especially if the dialogue underneath has already moved on. The better fix, when a line is genuinely too dense, is usually to shorten the wording rather than to stretch the timing.
